title: Only /0 is rejected; a set of very wide prefixes can still trust the whole world
evidence: parseTrustedElement rejects p.Bits()==0 but accepts e.g. TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS=0.0.0.0/1,128.0.0.0/1 (plus ::/1,8000::/1), which together cover every address and make XFF fully spoofable. Spec 3.1 only mandates the /0 check, so this is spec-conformant; it is an operator footgun, not a code bug.
fix: Optional: log a startup warning (or reject) for IPv4 prefixes shorter than /8 and IPv6 shorter than /16; or add it to the k8s-all policy test listed in spec 6 (never 0.0.0.0/0 or equivalent wide sets).

title: parseAddr is more lenient than spec 3.2: bracketed IPv4 and unvalidated ports are accepted
evidence: '[1.2.3.4]' and '[1.2.3.4]:80' are accepted as 1.2.3.4; net.SplitHostPort does not validate the port, so '1.2.3.4:abc' and '1.2.3.4:' are accepted as 1.2.3.4 instead of malformed. Not exploitable: only a trusted proxy controls the elements that are actually read (walk stops at the first untrusted), the key is the canonical Addr.String(), and the fuzz invariant still holds.
fix: Optional: require the bracket form only for IPv6 (a.Is6() after unbracketing) and require the port to be 1-5 decimal digits; add the cases to TestResolve. Acceptable to leave as is and record.

title: IPv6 clients are keyed per /128, so an attacker with a /64 can rotate addresses around the auth limit
evidence: rateKey uses ip:<resolved> with the full IPv6 address. Once XFF is honoured behind the ingress, a client holding a /64 (common for residential IPv6) gets 2^64 independent auth buckets. Pre-existing on develop for direct peers and explicitly out of scope of this spec (key classes unchanged), so not a regression.
fix: Follow-up task: key IPv6 auth/anonymous buckets by /64 (netip.PrefixFrom(a,64).Masked()); keep this change out of the current PR.
